is best applied to

structured.lead: The epithet "a comic epic in prose" is best applied to
structured.options_hint: Richardson's Pamela Sterne's A Sentiment

items.explanation: Henry Fielding famously defined the novel as a 'comic epic-poem in prose' in his 1742 Preface to Joseph Andrews, and brought this neoclassical comic epic form to its grandest realization in The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749).

items.explanation: Muriel Spark's second novel, Robinson (1958), is a dark, anti-utopian/dystopian castaway allegory in which three plane-crash survivors are stranded on a remote island ruled by its autocratic, reclusive owner, Miles Robinson.

items.explanation: Samuel Butler's Erewhon: or, Over the Range (1872)—whose title is an approximate anagram of 'nowhere'—is a classic work of Victorian Utopian (and satirical utopian) literature that lampoons British social, religious, and legal institutions.

items.title: Q4 · June 2010 (Paper II)

structured.options_hint: Byzantium Among School Children Sailing

items.explanation: The phrase 'monuments [printed here as moments] of unageing intellect' occurs in the first stanza of W. B. Yeats's poem 'Sailing to Byzantium' (published in The Tower, 1928), contrasting eternal artistic creation with mortal sensual life.

items.explanation: The Tree of Man (1955), Voss (1957), and The Vivisector (1970) are major novels by Australian Nobel Laureate Patrick White, whereas Oscar and Lucinda (1988) is a Booker Prize-winning historical novel by Australian writer Peter Carey.

structured.lead: The famous line "……. where ignorant armies clash by night" is taken from a poem by
structured.options_hint: Wilfred Owen Auden Siegfried Sassoon Mat

items.explanation: The famous closing line 'Where ignorant armies clash by night' comes from Matthew Arnold's Victorian lyric 'Dover Beach' (published in 1867), lamenting the ebbing of the 'Sea of Faith' and the spiritual confusion of the modern world.

structured.lead: The term 'theatre of cruelty' was coined by
structured.options_hint: Robert Brustein Antonin Artaud Augusto B

items.explanation: French avant-garde dramatist and theorist Antonin Artaud coined the term 'Theatre of Cruelty' (Théâtre de la Cruauté) in his manifestos collected in The Theatre and Its Double (1938), advocating visceral sensory performance to shock audiences out of complacency.

structured.options_hint: Milton Spenser Shakespeare Pope

items.explanation: Lord Byron composed his long narrative poem Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812–1818) in the nine-line Spenserian stanza (rhyming ababbcbcc and ending with an alexandrine), a verse form invented by Edmund Spenser for The Faerie Queene.

items.title: Q12 · June 2010 (Paper II)

structured.lead: Which post-war British poet was involved in a disastrous marriage with Sylvia Plath ?
structured.options_hint: Philip Larkin Ted Hughes Stevie Smith Ge

items.explanation: Post-war British Poet Laureate Ted Hughes married American confessional poet Sylvia Plath in June 1956. Their turbulent marriage ended in separation in 1962, shortly before Plath's tragic suicide in February 1963, which Hughes later addressed in Birthday Letters (1998).

items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer's dream-vision poem The Parliament of Fowles combines a beast fable of talking birds (IV), a St. Valentine's Day parliamentary debate over courtly love (II), and an unresolved demande d'amour or marital puzzle (I), rather than a threnody (funeral lament).

structured.options_hint: William Godwin Edmund Burke Thomas Paine

items.explanation: Anglo-American political activist and revolutionary theorist Thomas Paine wrote The Age of Reason; Being an Investigation of True and Fabulous Theology (published in three parts in 1794, 1795, and 1807), advocating Deism and rational critique of revealed religion.

items.title: Q15 · June 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
The Restoration comedy has been

structured.lead: The Restoration comedy has been criticized mainly for its
structured.options_hint: excessive wit and humour bitter satire a

items.explanation: From Jeremy Collier's 1698 polemic A Short View of the Immorality, and Profaneness of the English Stage through nineteenth-century Victorian critics like Lord Macaulay, Restoration comedy has been criticized mainly for its sexual indecency, cuckoldry plots, and moral permissiveness.

items.title: Q16 · June 2010 (Paper II)

items.explanation: 'Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses' (1970) is a foundational structuralist-Marxist essay by French philosopher Louis Althusser, introducing the concept of ideological 'interpellation' and distinguishing between Repressive and Ideological State Apparatuses.

items.title: Q17 · June 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Sexual possessiveness is a theme
of Shakespeare's

structured.lead: Sexual possessiveness is a theme of Shakespeare's
structured.options_hint: Coriolanus Julius Caesar Henry IV Part -

items.explanation: Sexual possessiveness, erotic jealousy, and patriarchal control over desire are central themes in William Shakespeare's comedy A Midsummer Night's Dream (c. 1595–1596), evident in Egeus's claim over Hermia, the tangled Athenian lovers, and Oberon and Titania's quarrel.

items.title: Q18 · June 2010 (Paper II)

structured.options_hint: Stephen Greenblatt Raymond Williams Matt

items.explanation: British Marxist critic Raymond Williams coined and developed the theory of 'Cultural Materialism' in works such as Marxism and Literature (1977) and Problems in Materialism and Culture (1980), viewing culture as a material, productive social and historical process.

items.explanation: Herman Northrop Frye (1912–1991) was a pre-eminent Canadian literary critic and theorist at the University of Toronto, renowned for his study of William Blake, Fearful Symmetry (1947), and his foundational work of archetypal criticism, Anatomy of Criticism (1957).

items.title: Q21 · June 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Sethe is a character in

structured.lead: Sethe is a character in
structured.options_hint: The Colour Purple The Women of Brewster

items.explanation: Sethe is the protagonist of Toni Morrison's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel Beloved (1987), an escaped enslaved mother living in post-Civil War Ohio whose house at 124 Bluestone Road is haunted by the spirit of the infant daughter she killed to save from slavery.

items.explanation: Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism (1983) is a seminal book by political scientist Benedict Anderson, arguing that nations are socially constructed 'imagined communities' fostered largely by 'print-capitalism.'

items.explanation: William Wycherley's Restoration comedy The Plain-Dealer (first performed in 1676) is a loose, darker adaptation of Molière's comedy Le Misanthrope (1666), with the blunt, misanthropic sea captain Manly modelled on Molière's Alceste.

structured.lead: 'Inversion' is the change in the word order for creating rhetorical effect, e.g. this book I like. Another term for inversion is
structured.options_hint: Hypallage Hubris Haiku Hyperbaton

items.explanation: Hyperbaton (from the Greek for 'transposition' or 'stepping over') is the classical rhetorical term for inversion—the deliberate rearrangement or departure from normal syntactic word order for emphasis or poetic effect.

items.explanation: Methodism, a major eighteenth-century evangelical revival movement within the Church of England emphasizing personal faith, methodical devotion, and social outreach, was founded by John Wesley along with his brother Charles Wesley and George Whitefield.

items.explanation: 'My First Acquaintance with Poets' (published in The Liberal in 1823) is a celebrated autobiographical essay by Romantic critic William Hazlitt, vividly recounting his youthful 1798 encounters with Samuel Taylor Coleridge and William Wordsworth.

items.explanation: Completed in 1611 by forty-seven scholars commissioned by King James I following the 1604 Hampton Court Conference, the King James Version (Authorized Version) of the Bible is universally regarded as the supreme monument of Jacobean English prose.

items.title: Q36 · June 2010 (Paper II)

items.explanation: The fog-shrouded English Court of Chancery is the central institutional and symbolic setting of Charles Dickens's novel Bleak House (1852–1853), which satirizes the ruinous delays of the equity legal system through the endless case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

items.title: Q37 · June 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth

structured.lead: Which romantic poet coined the famous phrase 'spots of time' ?
structured.options_hint: John Keats William Wordsworth Coleridge

items.explanation: William Wordsworth coined the phrase 'spots of time' in his autobiographical poem The Prelude (Book XI of the 1805 text; Book XII of the 1850 text) to describe vivid, formative childhood memories that retain a 'renovating virtue' to nourish the mind in later life.

items.explanation: In D. H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love (1920), the protagonist Rupert Birkin articulates the ideal of 'star-equilibrium' in his relationship with Ursula Brangwen—a union of 'two single equal stars balanced in conjunction' rather than suffocating romantic fusion.
